based cell-free conditions. Although the fold increase was modest (1.3-fold), it was
consistently above background and reproducible across multiple experimental
replicates, indicating the DNA amplification activity by phi29DNAP in the presence of
circular double-stranded plasmid.
To address this concern, we have added the following text in the revised manuscript
to emphasize that the observed replication was modest but reproducible, representing
a foundational step toward developing more robust DNA replication in lysate-based
cell-free systems.
Specifically, we now add the text as follows (Page 4):
“This modest (1.3-fold, Fig. 1b) but reproducible increase in DNA quantity indicates
that the LoopReX system supports limited DNA replication of circular plasmids under
current conditions, establishing a foundation for further optimization.”
6.3. In the sentence in page 4, “However, the DNA content in …”, the author wrote
“with DNA replication supporting the template synthesis continuously.” I did not
understand the logic of the author. Certainly, the fold changes were higher for LoopRex
system at all points in Fig 1c, but this can be because DNA replicated for LoopRex
system before 0.5 h and then DNA might stop replication and just degraded afterward.
In this case, template synthesis (i.e., DNA replication) did not proceed continuously.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. As you correctly point out, while the
LoopReX system showed higher DNA content than the control at all measured time
points in Fig. 1c, this does not necessarily prove continuous replication over time, and
we cannot rule out the possibility that DNA replication occurred predominantly during
an early time window (e.g., before 0.5 h), followed by degradation.
To make this clear and avoid misinterpretation, we have deleted “with DNA replication
supporting the template synthesis continuously” and revised the related text as follows
(Page 4):
“Specifically, DNA content remained high during the first hour and then gradually
decreased over the next five hours (Fig. 1c), likely due to nuclease-mediated
degradation in the cell lysate. Nonetheless, LoopReX consistently maintained higher
DNA levels than the control CFE system at all time points.”
6.4. The last sentence on page 5 contains the word “random,” which probably mentions
the nucleic acids present in the cell extract. I think that nucleic acids should be rRNA,
tRNA, mRNA, and fragments from the genome. They are never random. Please
rephrase it. More importantly, I could not understand the conclusion of Fig. S4,
“the nucleic acids present in the cell extract still effectively supported the synthesis of new
DNA strand.” To draw this conclusion, the author would need DNA replication
experiment with or without the nucleic acid in the cell extract, but there is no such data.
Initially, I thought Fig. S4C was the data, but the author wrote in the legend that the

Accordingly, I could not agree with the first sentence on page 6, “Our findings indicate

supplementary figures. I strongly recommend that the authors provide a more detailed
explanation of the Supplementary Figures.
Response: Thank you for the thoughtful and constructive comments. We agree that
the term “random” was imprecise in describing endogenous nucleic acids in the cell
extract. In the revised manuscript, we have replaced it with “diverse” to provide a more
accurate description.
Regarding our interpretation of Fig. S4 (now renumbered as Supplementary Figure 5),
we appreciate your critical evaluation and acknowledge that our original conclusion
was not sufficiently clear. In the original Fig. S4C, we compared ssM13 replication in
LoopReX reactions with (+) or without (–) the addition of specific primers. Notably,
replication still occurred in the absence of added primers (the “–” group), suggesting
that endogenous nucleic acids present in the extract could act as primers for DNA
replication. Based on this, we concluded that “the nucleic acids present in the cell
extract still effectively supported the synthesis of new DNA strands.”
To strengthen this conclusion, we performed additional validation experiments as you
suggested. Specifically, we purified endogenous nucleic acids from the cell extract and
added them to a defined, pure system-based DNA replication reaction containing
phi29DNAP and ssM13 template. Consistent with our hypothesis, purified endogenous
nucleic acids supported DNA replication, whereas no replication occurred in their
absence. Moreover, increasing the amount of nucleic acids enhanced DNA synthesis
(new data are provided in Figure R2). These results are now included in the updated
Supplementary Figure 5 (original Fig. S4), along with a revised figure legend for clarity
(please see Supplementary Information for more details). We hope that these new
experiments/data, together with the clarified explanation, adequately address your
concern and provide stronger support for our conclusion.
Figure R2. Replication of ssM13 in a defined (pure) reaction system. DNA replication

6.5. Page 8. What is ZGBoost models. A brief explanation is needed in the main text.
Response: Thank you for raising this point of clarification. We have now added a brief
explanation of XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting) and cited the original publication
describing XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016 – see Ref. 45) in the revised manuscript
as follows (Page 9):
“For in silico optimization, we employed XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting)45, a
decision tree-based ensemble method known for strong predictive performance,
scalability, and native handling of missing values and complex feature interactions.
Moreover, XGBoost mitigates overfitting and improves model generalization through
regularization, learning-rate shrinkage, subsampling of rows and columns, and early
stopping.”
Ref. 45: Chen, T. & Guestrin, C. XGBoost: a scalable tree boosting system. KDD’16:
In Proc. of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery
and Data Mining, 785-794 (2016).
6.6. Machine learning part. The explanation of the dataset used for machine learning
was insufficient. Please explain how the author got the data. Which factors changed?
How much did they change? How much data did they get?
Response: Thank you for these helpful comments. We have expanded the manuscript
to clarify how the data were generated, which factors were varied, and how the dataset
was constructed. The following text has been added to the revised manuscript (Page
10):
“We evaluated 16 factors (see “Factor selection and data processing” in Methods for
details), and all experimental data were generated in our laboratory. For model
development, the datasets comprised 115 experimental conditions for DNA replication
and 126 experimental conditions for protein expression, each representing a distinct
combination of reactants and their concentrations in the LoopReX system. Across
samples, the varying features were the identity and concentration of input reactants,
while all other experimental parameters were kept constant. The collected data were
randomly split, with 80% used for model training and 20% reserved for testing, and
five-fold cross-validation was performed to assess and enhance the robustness of our
models.”
7. Page 6. About the sentence, “Importantly, we also observed a remarkable increase
in protein express level… “, why did the protein expression increase? I would like to
know the author’s opinion.
Response: We appreciate your question and share the interest in understanding the
mechanism. We believe the increase in protein expression is primarily attributed to the
position and sequence features of the artificial origin within the plasmid (Fig. 1i, left).
This artificial origin, which is derived from the 3*φ10 promoter, appears to function as
an additional promoter recognized by T7 RNA polymerase. As a result, it drives the
transcription of more mRNA, thereby leading to higher protein expression compared
to the 3*φ10 promoter alone (Fig. 1i).
To test this hypothesis, we performed additional experiments during the revision (see
Figure R3, provided below for review only). Specifically, we compared mRNA levels
generated from plasmids containing either the 3*φ10 promoter or the artificial origin
(Arti-ori). After in vitro transcription, mRNA from both groups was converted into cDNA.
According to our model (Figure R3a), the 3*φ10 plasmid group produces only one type
of cDNA (cDNA-1), while the artificial origin-based plasmid (Arti-ori) can produce two
types (cDNA-1 and cDNA-2) due to the presence of a second transcription start site.
To distinguish these transcripts, we designed two primer pairs targeting different
regions in the cDNA. Primer-1 amplifies the sfGFP gene present in cDNA-1, whereas
primer-2 specifically amplifies the region between the artificial origin and the canonical
promoter in cDNA-2 (Figure R3a). We detected more primer-1 product from the Arti-
ori plasmid than from the 3*φ10 plasmid, and primer-2 products were observed only
with the Arti-ori plasmid. These results support our hypothesis that the artificial origin
enhances transcriptional output, which explains the increased protein expression.
While we cannot fully exclude additional contributions (e.g., mRNA stability or plasmid
architecture), our results point to transcriptional upregulation via the artificial origin
acting as an auxiliary T7 promoter as the primary cause of the increased protein yield.
Please note that Figure R3 is provided for your reference and is not included in the
main text or Supplementary Information.
Figure R3. Transcript analysis of the artificial origin-based plasmid (Arti-ori). a, Workflow
for transcript analysis via in vitro transcription, reverse transcription, and qPCR using two primer
pairs. b, Comparison of transcript levels generated from plasmids containing either the 3*φ10
promoter or the artificial origin (Arti-ori). Fold changes were determined by qPCR relative to the
reference 3*φ10-based plasmid. Data are presented as means, with error bars indicating the
standard deviation from three independent experiments (n = 3).
8. The replication of 3*phi10 was greater than 3, as shown in Fig. 1h, but 1 in Fig. 1i.
Why?
Response: Thank you for pointing out this source of confusion. In Fig. 1i, DNA
replication efficiencies of plasmids with different artificial origin positions were
compared after normalization to the control plasmid (3*φ10). For this reason, the
replication value of 3*φ10 appears as 1 in Fig. 1i, whereas in Fig. 1h the absolute fold
change is shown. We agree that the original y-axis label in Fig. 1i (“fold change”) was
misleading. To improve clarity, we have revised the label to “pJL1-T7-sfGFP replication
(normalized to 3*φ10).” Please see the updated Fig. 1i in the revised manuscript.
9. As shown in Figs. 2g and 2h, the improvements in LoopRex-Opt are seemingly small.
Is this unexpected result or reasonable? I’d like to know the author’s opinion.
Response: Thank you for this insightful observation. We agree that the improvements
in DNA replication and protein expression in LoopReX-Opt (Figs. 2g and 2h) are
moderate rather than dramatic. However, we believe these results are reasonable and
meaningful. In our machine learning-based optimization, two independent models
were developed to predict DNA replication and protein expression, respectively. The
effects of the selected formulations (F1-F5) on these two outputs did not always align.
For example, F5 yielded the lowest DNA replication efficiency but the second-highest
protein expression level (Figs. 2c and 2d). As a compromise, we selected formulation
F3 as the optimal condition (LoopReX-Opt) for balancing coupled DNA replication and
protein expression.
Although the overall improvements are moderate (Figs. 2g and 2h), LoopReX-Opt
consistently outperformed LoopReX-Ori. Importantly, protein expression efficiency
was notably enhanced: LoopReX-Opt reached maximum protein yield after only 3
hours (Fig. 2h), nearly 2-fold higher than LoopReX-Ori at the same time point. This
acceleration is meaningful as it enables LoopReX-Opt to serve as a more efficient
platform for producing target molecules, such as cellular components for artificial cell
construction.
To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the revised manuscript (Page
12):
“Although the improvements in DNA replication and protein expression were moderate
(Fig. 2g,h), these results reflect the complex interplay of reaction components in
LoopReX and demonstrate the utility of machine learning for optimizing such
multifactorial systems. Importantly, LoopReX-Opt accelerates genetic information
transfer and provides a more efficient TTcDR framework, which could be valuable for
advancing artificial life research.”
10. Fig. 4f. The protein expression yield for Unmodified IdsDNA was much lower than
previous data (e.g., Fig. 2h). Why?
Response: Thank you for this important observation. The low protein expression yield
observed for “Unmodified ldsDNA” (Fig. 4f) is attributable to the low amount of DNA
template retained in the reaction. During nucleoid preparation, DNA templates were
incubated with artificial nucleoids and then washed three times to remove unbound
DNA (see Methods, “Preparation and recovery of artificial nucleoids”). Because
unmodified ldsDNA lacks biotin, it could not be efficiently anchored to the nucleoids,
leaving only small amounts of nonspecifically bound DNA available for protein
expression. This explains the markedly lower yield observed in Fig. 4f.
To confirm this, we conducted additional experiments to measure binding efficiencies
of different ldsDNA templates. We found that all three types of biotin-modified ldsDNA
templates exhibited nearly 100% binding efficiency, whereas unmodified ldsDNA
displayed substantially lower binding, consistent with nonspecific interactions (see
below Figure R4). These results have now been included in the Supplementary
Information (Supplementary Figure 13).
In addition, we have added the following clarification to the revised manuscript (Pages
16-17):
“We first evaluated the binding efficiency of DNA templates to artificial nucleoids and
found that all biotin-modified templates bound with nearly 100% efficiency, whereas
unmodified ldsDNA showed markedly lower binding efficiency, likely due to nonspecific
interactions (Supplementary Fig. 13).”

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This article presents a thorough proof of concept that a minimal circuit for DNA
replication can be designed and iterated upon in E. coli lysate. Trying to expand cell
free to beyond just in vitro transcription and translation to extend to replication is
conceptually useful, and this is a thoroughly completed proof of concept involving
machine learning, demonstration of improved DNA replication, and
compartmentalization, and demonstration that it can improve the concentration of
reporter proteins.
A few comments, that are mostly high level, but I think a large re-write adjusting the
framing is necessary for publication.
Response: We sincerely thank you for evaluating our manuscript and for your valuable
comments and positive assessment of the concept and strengths of our work. We
greatly appreciate your recognition of our efforts to extend cell-free systems beyond
transcription and translation by incorporating a minimal DNA replication circuit. We
have carefully considered your suggestions and have addressed your comments point-
by-point below.
1. Framing it as “artificial central dogma” complete obfuscates the entire premise of
the article. Canonically, the central dogma refers to the flow of information in cells
(DNA-->RNA-->Proteins) which certainly happens in any lysate or PURExpress-based
TXTL system wherein transcription and translation are necessary to transfer
information. Replication is important for cells, but I don’t think this is generally what
people think of when they consider the central dogma of biology. For this reason I think
“reconstituting artificial central dogma” feels confusing and somewhat jargon-y and
makes it harder for the reader to digest this information. I think a concept of the central
dogma that includes regeneration and self-replication has come into dialogue in part
of the synthetic biology/origins of life/artificial cells community, but it is not widely used
language in the broader synthetic biology community, much other areas of molecular
biology.
I recommend that throughout the manuscript, “artificial central dogma” is replaced with
more precise language. I also recommend a title change.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback. We fully agree
that the canonical definition of the central dogma refers to the flow of information from
DNA to RNA to proteins. We understand that framing our study using the term “artificial
central dogma” may lead to confusion, especially as this terminology is not widely used
across the broader molecular biology and synthetic biology communities.
To improve clarity, we have replaced all instances of “artificial central dogma” in the
manuscript with more accurate and specific phrases such as “transcription–translation-
coupled DNA replication (TTcDR)”. In line with your recommendation, we have also
updated the manuscript title to “Reconstituting transcription–translation-coupled DNA
replication within complex in vitro biological systems” to improve the accessibility for a
broader readership.
2. Related—on page 2 there is a discussion of the PURExpress system and its
limitations:
“Elements)-based cell-free expression system, which operates within a well-defined
(bio)chemical environment6, has been widely used to construct artificial life systems7-
9. However, these systems often exhibit only individual life characteristics, for example,
self-replication (e.g., DNA replication)7-12, self-evolution13-15, cell division16-18,
communication19-23, or metabolism25. Essentially, PURE system represents a
relatively simplified platform for in vitro biology.”
I may be misunderstanding the point of this sentence but how can PURExpress
systems replicate cell division outside of the cell. I believe the point was to say that
individual components of life can be replicated, but it is challenging to put it all together,
but I would recommend a major rewrite of this section for clarity.
Response: Thank you for highlighting this ambiguity in our original text. Our intention
was to emphasize that the PURE system has been successfully applied to reconstitute
specific, individual life-like processes, but that combining these functions into a unified
artificial system remains very challenging. We recognize that our original phrasing —
particularly references to “self-evolution,” “cell division,” and “communication” — could
be misinterpreted as suggesting that the PURE system fully replicates these complex
processes, which was not our intent.
To improve clarity, we have revised the text as follows (Page 2):
“The PURE (Protein synthesis Using Recombinant Elements)-based cell-free
expression system, which functions in a well-defined (bio)chemical environment6,
has been widely applied to reconstitute specific life-like processes such as DNA
replication7-12, gene sequence evolution13-15, cell division-like events16-18, artificial–
natural cell communication19-23, and light-driven ATP regeneration24. However, these
efforts typically address isolated functions, and integrating multiple life characteristics
into a single artificial system remains a major challenge given the relatively simplified
nature of the PURE platform.”
3. Overall, I caveat the authors on boldly claiming concepts are “confirmed” when they
are merely supported. An example of this can be found on page 6
“These findings confirm our hypothesis that the position of the promoters (i.e., the
artificial origin) plays a crucial role in regulating DNA replication and transcription”
I think the word “support” would be better than “confirm”. Given the toy system nature
of this investigation, it is difficult to say how it reacts in more complex situations. It’s
just one piece of evidence supporting this hypothesis.
Another example of this can be found on page 20. Did the authors indicate that
compartmentalization is “essential”. I feel this work just shows that it is beneficial and
improves protein production, not that this cannot occur without it. The controls
demonstrate that this replication can occur, just less efficiently.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback. We appreciate
your suggestions and have revised the relevant sentences to more accurately reflect
the scope of our findings and to avoid overstatements.
Specifically, we have changed the text on Page 6 to:
“These findings support our hypothesis that the position of the promoters (i.e., the
artificial origin) plays a crucial role in regulating DNA replication and transcription.”
Additionally, the statement on Page 22 now reads:
“This spatial compartmentalization is beneficial for efficient DNA replication...”
4. In Supplementary Figure 10 and Figure 4c could use a clearer explanation of why
morphology observed for DNA complexes is lighter and what the TEM is measuring,
and perhaps a reference for the method—essentially since this is such an
interdisciplinary field, it should walk the reader through these experiments.
Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have clarified in the Methods and
figure legends how contrast is generated in negative-stain TEM. In bright-field TEM,
darker regions correspond to areas enriched with heavy-atom stain (uranyl acetate),
which scatter more electrons, while lighter regions correspond to stain-excluded areas
that transmit more electrons. DNA-rich condensates typically exclude uranyl acetate
from their interior, resulting in an electron-lucent (lighter) morphology with darker rims
at the boundaries where stain accumulates. This appearance is consistent with the
expected behavior of nucleic acids and proteins under negative-stain conditions.
To make this clear, we have added the following text to the legends of Figure 4c and
Supplementary Figure 10 and a reference on negative staining (De Carlo and Harris,
Micron, 2011, 42, 117-131) as follows:
“Protein–DNA complexes appear lighter under TEM, likely because DNA-rich
condensates exclude uranyl acetate stain from their interior, resulting in lower contrast
compared to protein alone51.” (Page 18)
Ref. 51: De Carlo, S. & Harris, J. R. Negative staining and cryo-negative staining of
macromolecules and viruses for TEM. Micron 42, 117-131 (2011).
In addition, we have added a description of the TEM method in the revised manuscript
(Page 32):
“Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
TEM images were acquired using a JEOL JEM-1400 Plus microscope at an operating
voltage of 120 kV. Samples (10 μL of artificial nucleoids resuspended in nuclease-free
water) were deposited on a carbon-coated copper grid (300 mesh), excess liquid was
removed by filter paper after 1 min, and the grids were air-dried. Negative staining was
performed with 2% uranyl acetate (10 μL, 30 s), followed by air-drying before imaging.”

to deposit Juptyr notebooks on GitHub.
Response: Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We apologize for the omission.
In the revised manuscript, we have included the “Code availability” section as follows
(Page 33). We also updated the machine learning checklist for your reference.
“Code availability
All codes used for model development and analysis have been deposited in GitHub
and can be accessed at https://github.com/BMG-FDU/XGBoost_model.git.”

value and novelty of our study. We greatly appreciate your constructive comments and
have carefully considered and addressed each of your concerns point-by-point below.
1. Although the study revealed the synergistic effect of T7RNAP and phi29DNAP in
DNA replication, the specific molecular mechanism remains to be further explored. It
is suggested that biochemical analysis or structural biology methods should be used
to further elucidate the specific roles of these enzymes in the replication process. For
example, ‘forming a replication initiation complex for DNA replication’ (Fig.1g), the
complex should be considered.
Response: Thank you for your insightful suggestions. We agree that further elucidation
of the molecular mechanisms underlying the synergistic effect between T7RNAP and
phi29DNAP, particularly regarding the formation of a replication initiation complex,
would significantly enhance our understanding.
In our current study, we specifically examined how and where primers are generated
to initiate replication. Previous studies have shown that T7RNAP can produce different
RNA products depending on the promoter, including full-length mRNA and abortive
transcripts (typically 3-8 nucleotides). To investigate this, we constructed plasmids with
different promoters and observed that T7RNAP and specific promoters indeed
facilitated replication initiation, although the efficiency varied among different
promoters (Fig. 1f). In addition, to address whether endogenous nucleic acids from the
cell extract could serve as primers, we performed new experiments during the revision.
We purified endogenous nucleic acids and added them to a defined in vitro DNA
replication system containing phi29DNAP and an ssM13 template. We found that
these nucleic acids supported DNA replication, and increasing their concentration
enhanced DNA synthesis (see Figure R5 below). Without endogenous nucleic acids,
we observed no replication. These results are now included in Supplementary Figure
5 (original Fig. S4).
Figure R5. Replication of ssM13 in a defined (pure) reaction system. DNA replication
reactions were performed using phi29DNAP, ssM13 template, and purified endogenous nucleic
acids (background nucleic acids, BNAs). The results demonstrate that BNAs isolated from the
cell extract can function as primers to initiate DNA replication. No replication was observed in
the absence of BNAs, whereas increasing BNA concentrations supported higher levels of DNA
synthesis. Data are presented as means, with error bars indicating the standard deviation from
three independent experiments (n = 3).
Additionally, we have conducted further biochemical assays to determine whether
there is a direct interaction between T7RNAP and phi29DNAP in our reaction system.
We first performed a pull-down assay by purifying phi29DNAP from the LoopReX
reaction. SDS-PAGE analysis revealed no T7RNAP band in the pull-down sample,
indicating the absence of a stable T7RNAP–phi29DNAP complex (see Figure R6
below). We then carried out isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) by titrating
phi29DNAP into T7RNAP, and again found no detectable binding affinity (see Figure
R7 below). These results suggest that T7RNAP and phi29DNAP do not directly interact
in our system. Please note that Figures R6 and R7 are provided for your reference and
are not included in the main text or Supplementary Information.
Figure R6. SDS-PAGE analysis of T7RNAP and phi29DNAP following the pull-down
assay. In the “Pull down” lane, only the protein band corresponding to phi29DNAP is visible.
The “Standard” lanes show the purified T7RNAP and phi29DNAP, respectively.
Figure R7. ITC assay of the interaction between T7RNAP and phi29DNAP. phi29DNAP (50
μM) was titrated into T7RNAP (5 μM), and no heat release was detected, which indicates no
interaction between phi29DNAP and T7RNAP.
Regarding the phrase “forming a replication initiation complex for DNA replication (Fig.
1g),” we agree that, as we have no direct experimental evidence, it may be misleading.
Therefore, we have removed this statement from the revised manuscript (Page 5).
2. The current system is mainly focused on DNA replication and protein expression,
and more cellular functions such as metabolic pathways and signal transduction can
be considered.
Response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We share your interest in extending
the system to incorporate additional cellular functions. In our original submission (Fig.
5b-d), we demonstrated that artificial nucleoids functionalized with the enzyme LacZ
could catalyze the conversion of o-nitrophenyl-β-D-galactopyranoside (ONPG) into o-
nitrophenol (ONP). Following your suggestion, we performed additional experiments
to reconstitute a two-enzyme metabolic pathway for the biotransformation of styrene
into (S)-1-phenyl-1,2-ethanediol. Specifically, two enzymes, StyA and SpEH, were co-
expressed and self-assembled into artificial nucleoids, enabling efficient conversion of
styrene to the desired product. These results are now included in Supplementary
Figure 14 (see Figure R8 below).
We have also added the following text to the revised manuscript (Page 19):
“Additionally, we successfully constructed a two-enzyme metabolic pathway by co-
expressing StyA (the oxygenase subunit of styrene monooxygenase) and SpEH
(epoxide hydrolase)27 with CipB-streptavidin, which self-assembled into artificial
nucleoids and catalyzed the conversion of styrene into (S)-1-phenyl-1,2-ethanediol
(Supplementary Fig. 14).”
As our main objective was to reconstitute DNA replication and protein expression in a
complex in vitro system, we did not extend our study to include artificial cell
construction or signal transduction in this work. Nonetheless, we agree that expanding
LoopReX to support such higher-order cellular functions is an exciting direction, and
we plan to pursue this in future studies.
Figure R8. Reconstitution of a two-enzyme metabolic pathway in LoopReX. a, Schematic
of the pathway for conversion of styrene to (S)-1-phenyl-1,2-ethanediol. StyA, the oxygenase
subunit of styrene monooxygenase; SpEH, epoxide hydrolase. b, De novo synthesized artificial
nucleoids incorporating StyA and SpEH enzymes in LoopReX. c, High-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) analysis of standard (top), negative control reaction without DNA
templates (middle), and reaction sample (bottom).
3. Besides being faster, what other advantages does LoopReX have? Where does
more DNA than CFE flow? (Fig.1d)
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. In Figs. 1c and 1d, we compared
DNA replication and protein expression between the initial LoopReX system and a
traditional CFE system. We observed that LoopReX consistently outperformed CFE in
both aspects. Specifically, DNA replication in LoopReX was about two-fold higher than
in CFE (Fig. 1c), providing the foundation and motivation for further optimization. In
addition, protein expression in LoopReX proceeded more rapidly, reaching its peak at
least one hour earlier than in CFE within the 6-hour window (Fig. 1d). After machine
learning-guided optimization, the enhanced LoopReX-Opt system achieved maximum
protein yield within just 3 hours, which is substantially faster than the original LoopReX
(8 hours; Fig. 2h) and CFE (14 hours; Supplementary Fig. 9). We believe this
accelerated protein expression is a key advantage of LoopReX, particularly for
applications requiring efficiency and high throughput.
Regarding more DNA levels in LoopReX, we note that DNA content still decreased
after the first hour (Fig. 1c), indicating that DNA degradation occurs in both systems.
However, the transiently elevated DNA levels in LoopReX likely contributed to the
faster protein expression observed in Fig. 1d.
To clarify this in the manuscript, we have revised the text as follows (Page 5):
“Additionally, protein expression in LoopReX reached its maximum earlier than in the
control CFE system, suggesting a faster expression rate that offers advantages in
efficiency and throughput. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that LoopReX
outperforms the CFE system in both DNA replication and protein expression, providing
a robust platform for subsequent optimization.”
4. In machine learning, is the division of the training set and the test set random? What
is the basis of the division?
Response: Thank you for the helpful comment. Yes, the division of the training (80%)
and test (20%) sets was performed randomly to ensure that both are representative of
the overall data distribution and to minimize selection bias. To further improve
reproducibility and statistical robustness, we employed five-fold cross-validation during
model development. All random splits were conducted with a fixed random seed to
maintain consistency across repeated experiments.
To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the revised manuscript (Page
10):
“We evaluated 16 factors (see “Factor selection and data processing” in Methods for
details), and all experimental data were generated in our laboratory. For model
development, the datasets comprised 115 experimental conditions for DNA replication
and 126 experimental conditions for protein expression, each representing a distinct
combination of reactants and their concentrations in the LoopReX system. Across
samples, the varying features were the identity and concentration of input reactants,
while all other experimental parameters were kept constant. The collected data were
randomly split, with 80% used for model training and 20% reserved for testing, and
five-fold cross-validation was performed to assess and enhance the robustness of our
models.”
5. In Figure 3b, the increase of DNA mass is due to the continuous enlargement of the
system or the continuous iteration of culture?
Response: Thank you for this question. As shown in Fig. 3a, continuous iteration
through serial dilutions enabled sustained DNA amplification. Building on this, in Fig.
3b we performed successive saturated iterative reactions, where the entire reaction
mixture from the previous round was used as a seed to inoculate fresh reactions at a
fixed 1:3 ratio (seed:fresh mix). Thus, the observed increase in DNA mass in Fig. 3b
reflects continuous iteration of the culture, with replicated DNA serving as templates
for protein expression. We then calculated the cumulative theoretical protein yields
across iterative rounds (Fig. 3b, right).
To make this clear, we have added the following text to the legend of Fig. 3b (Page
15):
“Seed DNA from the previous round was carried into the next round (1:3 ratio) to
enable iterative amplification and serve as templates for protein expression.”
6. In Figure 3c, what are the key differences between in vitro amplification and small
trials? Is the effect equal amplification?
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. The key differences between in
vitro amplification and small trials are (i) the reaction scale and (ii) protein yield per
initial DNA input. In vitro amplification uses iterative rounds to scale up to larger
volumes (e.g., 1 mL), whereas small trials are single-batch reactions (15 µL) without
amplification. Importantly, starting from the same DNA input, protein yields per DNA
input were approximately 10-fold higher in in vitro amplification compared to small trials,
demonstrating that this approach both conserves DNA and enhances overall product
yield.
To clarify this in the manuscript, we have revised the text as follows (Page 14):
“Specifically, protein yields per DNA input in (i) single- and (ii) double-amplification
reactions (up to 1 mL) increased by 9.5- and 15-fold, respectively, compared to the
standard 15 µL LoopReX-Opt reaction. This indicates that in vitro amplification not only
reduces DNA input requirements but also substantially enhances overall product yield.”
7. Does artificial nucleoid perform other functions, such as signal transduction? What
are the properties of artificial nucleoid, solid or liquid?
Response: Thank you for these insightful questions. As noted in our response to your
comment 2, the primary aim of our current study was to reconstitute DNA replication
and protein expression in a complex in vitro system; we did not extend our investigation
to artificial cell construction or signal transduction in this work. Nevertheless, we agree
that exploring the potential of artificial nucleoids for higher-order cellular functions is a
promising direction and plan to pursue this in future studies.
To demonstrate additional functionality of artificial nucleoids, during the revision we
conducted new experiments reconstituting a two-enzyme metabolic pathway by co-
expressing StyA (the oxygenase subunit of styrene monooxygenase) and SpEH
(epoxide hydrolase) with CipB-streptavidin. The resulting artificial nucleoids efficiently
catalyzed the conversion of styrene to (S)-1-phenyl-1,2-ethanediol. These findings are
provided in Supplementary Figure 14 (please see above Figure R8 and our response
to comment 2 for details).
Regarding the properties of artificial nucleoids, CipB (the bacterial protein used in their
construction) is known to form insoluble protein crystalline inclusions. CipB-mediated
aggregation is therefore solid rather than liquid. In our experiments, CipB readily
formed solid structures ranging from nanoscale to microscale particles (see Fig. 4c
and 4d), consistent with previous reports (Refs. 48-50). Artificial nucleoids were also
recoverable by centrifugation as solid pellets in our study.
For clarity, we have revised the text in the manuscript as follows (Page 16):
“Upon adding DNA, the protein-DNA complex formed similar nano-compartments (Fig.
4c, right; Supplementary Fig. 11), resulting in artificial nucleoids. These structures
further aggregated into protein-DNA clusters, visible as solid, green particles with
FAM-labeled DNA (Fig. 4d).”
8. What is the reason of ‘higher protein concentrations provided enhanced DNA
protection’?
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. Previous studies, including our own,
have shown that linear DNA templates in lysate-based cell-free systems can be
protected from nuclease degradation by DNA-binding proteins or immobilization (Zhu
et al., Biotechnol. Bioeng. 2020, 117, 3849-3857; Yim et al, ACS Synth. Biol. 2020, 9,
2851-2855; Norouzi et al., ACS Synth. Biol. 2021, 10, 1615-1624; Lu et al., ACS
Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2024, 12, 18219-18230). In our system, higher protein
concentrations enhanced DNA protection because CipB binds DNA and promotes the
assembly of artificial nucleoids. At elevated CipB levels, DNA is more effectively
coated and compacted, which shields it from nuclease degradation in the cell extract.
This protection helps maintain DNA integrity for subsequent amplification and protein
synthesis.
To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the revised manuscript (Page
16):
“This effect is likely due to increased CipB concentrations promoting more efficient
coating and compaction of DNA into artificial nucleoids, which in turn shields DNA from
nuclease degradation in the cell extract, as reported in previous studies36,52-54.”
Ref. 36: Lu, Y. et al. Chitin-functionalized cell-free system enables sustainable
biocatalysis and gene expression. ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 12, 18219-18230
(2024).
Ref. 52: Zhu, B. et al. Increasing cell-free gene expression yields from linear templates
in Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens extracts by using DNA-binding proteins.
Biotechnol. Bioeng. 117, 3849-3857 (2020).
Ref. 53: Yim, S. S., Johns, N. I., Noireaux, V. & Wang, H. H. Protecting linear DNA
templates in cell-free expression systems from diverse bacteria. ACS Synth. Biol. 9,
2851-2855 (2020).
Ref. 54: Norouzi, M., Panfilov, S. & Pardee, K. High-efficiency protection of linear DNA
in cell-free extracts from Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens. ACS Synth. Biol. 10,
1615-1624 (2021).
9. In Figure 4e and 4f, the efficiency of DNA and protein synthesis is not quite the same,
what are the possible reasons?
Response: Thank you for this constructive comment. We believe the differences in
efficiencies observed with DNA replication (Fig. 4e) and protein synthesis (Fig. 4f) arise
mainly from the binding format of DNA to CipB-assembled scaffolds. Dual-biotin-
modified DNA performed best, as both ends were anchored to CipB, which provided
strong protection from nuclease degradation and supported efficient template
amplification for protein synthesis. In contrast, single-biotin-modified DNA, with one
end exposed to nucleases, was more prone to degradation, leading to reduced
replication and lower protein synthesis efficiency.
To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the revised manuscript (Page
17):
“While the overall performance of TTcDR was improved with DNA-loaded artificial
nucleoids, the efficiencies varied depending on the DNA–CipB binding format. Dual-
biotin-modified DNA achieved the highest efficiency, as both ends were protected by
CipB binding, preventing degradation and enabling more templates for protein
synthesis. In contrast, single-biotin-modified DNA, with one free end exposed to
nucleases, was more readily degraded, resulting in lower DNA replication and protein
synthesis efficiency.”
10. How can it be shown that DNA replication occurs on a nucleoid and transcription
occurs in liquid?
Response: Thank you for this valuable comment. To construct artificial nucleoids, DNA
was initially loaded onto CipB-assembled scaffolds and was only detected on these
nucleoids at the start of the reaction (Fig. 4e, yellow bars at 0 h). After DNA replication,
the newly synthesized DNA, lacking biotin-modified ends, could not bind to the CipB
scaffolds and was released into the supernatant, where it then served as templates for
transcription and translation in the liquid phase. Our original text was intended to
convey this hypothesized spatial separation. However, as we have not performed
direct experiments to confirm this, we have deleted the relevant statement to avoid
misinterpretation.
The following sentence has been removed from the revised manuscript:
“The findings also indicate that artificial nucleoids enable spatial separation of DNA
replication (which occurs on the nucleoids) and transcription-translation (which occurs
in the liquid cytoplasm-like environment), thereby facilitating an efficient flow of genetic
information.”
11. In Figure 5a, how can we undo the effect of non-karyon expression in vivo?
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. Since we did not conduct
experiments in vivo, we assume your question refers to non-karyon expression in vitro
as shown in Fig. 5a.
In our system, newly replicated, unmodified DNA is released into the liquid phase and
can also serve as templates for protein expression. To minimize carryover, after each
round the hybrid artificial nucleoids (composed of CipB-streptavidin, CipB-mCherry,
and dual-biotin-modified DNA) are collected, washed, and resuspended for the next
round of reaction (see “Preparation and recovery of artificial nucleoids” in Methods).
This process removes unbound DNA, ensuring that only nucleoid-bound DNA template
is carried forward to subsequent DNA replication and protein synthesis in the next
round, thereby reducing non-karyon expression from previous rounds. However,
during each new reaction cycle, freshly synthesized DNA in the liquid phase can still
serve as templates for protein expression and cannot be eliminated during the ongoing
process.
To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the legend of Fig. 5a (Page
20):
“After each round, hybrid artificial nucleoids composed of CipB-streptavidin, CipB-
mCherry, and dual-biotin-modified DNA were collected, washed, and resuspended for
the next round of reaction (see “Preparation and recovery of artificial nucleoids” in
Methods). This process removed free unmodified DNA, so that only nucleoid-bound
DNA templates were carried forward into the next round of DNA replication and protein
expression.”
12. Is it the order of transcription and then replication in vitro? Is the translation process
sequential? Is there any representation of translation? Is it transcription and translation?
What if it's a eukaryotic system?
Response: Thank you for these insightful questions. As proposed in Fig. 1g, T7RNAP
can generate two types of RNA products: (i) short abortive transcripts that serve as
primers for phi29DNAP-mediated DNA replication, and (ii) full-length mRNAs that
serve as templates for translation. In this context, transcription can provide primers
that initiate replication. However, we also observed that endogenous nucleic acids
present in the cell extract could act as primers, enabling phi29DNAP to initiate
replication even without transcription-derived RNAs. Meanwhile, full-length mRNAs
produced by T7RNAP are translated by the cell extract machinery.
Thus, in our in vitro LoopReX system, replication, transcription, and translation are not
strictly sequential but occur in a coupled and partially overlapping manner. We
emphasize that LoopReX functions as a coupled system rather than a strictly ordered
pathway, with the three processes taking place in parallel and influencing each other.
LoopReX integrates four core modules: (1) phi29DNAP, (2) T7RNAP, (3) E. coli cell
extract, and (4) artificial nucleoids, which together coordinate replication, transcription,
and translation.
Regarding eukaryotic systems, we agree that a eukaryotic cell extract could, in
principle, be integrated with the other modules to establish a eukaryotic version of
LoopReX. Exploring such extensions is an exciting future direction that could broaden
the applicability of our platform. We have discussed this point in the main text as
follows: “Additionally, while LoopReX is based on E. coli crude extracts, future work
could explore adapting the system to other cell types or organisms, which would
require further optimization to fully harness the potential of diverse biological
components.” (Page 23)
13. What are the advantages of scaling up protein production compared to in vivo, in
terms of cost and time?
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful comment. We agree that it is important to
consider the advantages of LoopReX compared to in vivo systems in terms of cost and
time. Unlike in vivo systems, where protein expression requires multiple steps
including cell cultivation, genetic transformation, and optimization of culture conditions,
LoopReX enables direct in vitro protein synthesis from DNA templates. This approach
eliminates the need for time-consuming cell growth and scale-up, allowing proteins to
be produced within hours rather than days.
Furthermore, LoopReX streamlines rapid prototyping and testing of DNA constructs,
removing the need for labor-intensive cloning and the maintenance of living cells. This
significantly reduces both the labor and costs associated with strain engineering and
cell-based workflows. Another key advantage is the iterative amplification capability of
LoopReX, which lowers the initial DNA template requirements and maximizes protein
yield per unit of DNA.
The cost-effectiveness of LoopReX can be further enhanced by recent developments:
our group and the Jewett laboratory have employed machine learning- and design-
driven strategies to optimize cell-free reagent formulations, substantially reducing the
cost of cell-free gene expression (Zhu et al., Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 2720; Olsen et
al., bioRxiv preprint doi: https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.08.01.668204).
Taken together, these features confer clear advantages to LoopReX in terms of speed,
flexibility, and efficiency, especially for rapid prototyping, high-throughput screening,
and applications where in vivo protein production is hampered by toxicity or metabolic
burden.
To clarify this in the manuscript, we have added the following text (Page 22):
“Additional advantages of LoopReX include significant time savings and cost-
effectiveness compared to in vivo protein production. Unlike in vivo systems, LoopReX
bypasses cloning and cell cultivation, enabling protein synthesis directly from DNA
within hours. Furthermore, when paired with recent machine learning-optimized cell-
free formulations that further reduce cost47, LoopReX will provide a rapid, flexible, and
scalable platform well-suited for prototyping and high-throughput applications.”
14. What are the intracellular and extracellular aggregation conditions of CipB? Which
conditions can achieve the best aggregation effect?
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. CipB is a bacterial crystalline
inclusion protein known to self-assemble into scaffolds in various hosts such as
Photorhabdus luminescens and E. coli (Refs. 48-50). Previous studies have shown
that CipB–enzyme fusion proteins form stable inclusion complexes for efficient
biocatalysis. In our current study, CipB was expressed directly in the LoopReX system
rather than in vivo, and we confirmed successful aggregation under in vitro conditions.
Although we did not systematically compare intracellular versus extracellular assembly,
both our data and prior reports support that CipB readily self-assembles across diverse
in vivo and in vitro environments.
To further assess in vitro aggregation, we examined CipB aggregates in PBS buffer
and pure water during the revision. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis indicated
that CipB formed stable aggregates with similar morphologies under both conditions
(Figure R9). Please note that Figure R9 is provided for your reference only and is not
included in the main text or Supplementary Information.
Figure R9. AFM analysis of CipB aggregates under PBS buffer and pure water conditions.
CipB was expressed in LoopReX, purified, and resuspended in different buffers, showing
comparable morphologies.
15. Whether the activity of the enzyme or protein after aggregation with cipB has been
changed? Whether the folding of the protein or enzyme has been affected from soluble
to insoluble? Authors should include some predictive data on the effect of CipB on the
structure of the target enzyme or protein, such as using AlphaFold3.
Response: We appreciate this insightful comment. To minimize potential interference,
we introduced a peptide linker (nine amino acids) between CipB and LacZ in the fusion
construct (Supplementary Table 1). During revision, we directly compared the catalytic
activities of LacZ and CipB-LacZ. Both enzymes displayed comparable activities and
similar catalytic profiles (Figure R10), consistent with previous studies showing that
CipB fusion does not impair enzyme activity (Refs. 48-50). These results suggest that
CipB assembly does not adversely affect enzyme folding or function.
In addition, we used AlphaFold3 to predict the structures of LacZ and CipB-LacZ. The
predicted LacZ domain in the fusion construct overlapped nearly perfectly with wild-
type LacZ (Figure R11), further supporting that CipB does not alter LacZ folding.
To clarify these points, we have included Figures R10 and R11 (now Supplementary
Figs. 26 and 27) in Supplementary Information and added the following text to the
manuscript (Page 32):
“Comparison of enzymatic activities and structural predictions of CipB-LacZ versus
LacZ are provided in Supplementary Figs. 26 and 27, respectively.”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors appropriately responded to my comments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: All comments were adequately addressed in this revision
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I still have some concern for the revised manuscript.
1. In the absence of DNA replication, the protein expression efficiency also increased. However, when comparing 2d and 2f, no obvious increase in expression efficiency was observed. What could be the possible reasons for this?
2. Does the mutual influence between DNA replication and protein expression get resolved? What is the optimal expression method? What does the optimal expression method indicate as the most significant influencing factor? Is this related to the length of DNA primers and the type of expressed proteins?
3. How is cross-validation specifically applied in the machine learning part? Is it five-fold cross-validation on the entire dataset, and then the average performance of cross-validation is taken as the final result? Or is it first divided into 80/20, and then five-fold cross-validation is performed on the training set?
4. If the test set contains conditions that are highly similar to those in the training set (for example, different concentrations of the same reactant), the model performance may be overestimated. Although the R² value is high, the ratio of the number of features to the sample size may be too high, which can easily lead to overfitting. Are there better methods for dividing the training set and test set?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-point response to reviewer comments:
Comments in italics
Responses in blue
Changes in the body of the manuscript are noted in red.
Reviewer Comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors appropriately responded to my comments.
Response: Thank you.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
All comments were adequately addressed in this revision.
Response: Thank you.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I still have some concern for the revised manuscript.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your time and effort in reviewing our manuscript.
Your previous insightful and constructive comments have greatly improved the quality
and clarity of our work. We appreciate your re-evaluation of the revised version and
address your remaining concerns point-by-point below.
1. In the absence of DNA replication, the protein expression efficiency also increased.
However, when comparing 2d and 2f, no obvious increase in expression efficiency was
observed. What could be the possible reasons for this?
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. The key difference of Figs. 2d and
2f is that protein expression in Fig. 2d was coupled with DNA replication, whereas in
Fig. 2f it was not. The data indicate that the overall protein expression efficiency in Fig.
2f was slightly lower than in Fig. 2d. We believe this is likely because the newly
replicated DNA in the LoopReX reactions (Fig. 2d) can also serve as additional
templates for transcription and translation, leading to even higher protein yields
compared with reactions lacking DNA replication (Fig. 2f).
To clarify this point, we have added the following text to the revised manuscript (Page
11):
“However, it is worth noting that the protein expression efficiency without DNA
replication (Fig. 2f) was overall lower than that in LoopReX reactions with DNA
replication (Fig. 2d). This difference is likely because the newly synthesized DNA in
LoopReX can also serve as templates for protein expression, thereby enhancing
protein yields.”
2. Does the mutual influence between DNA replication and protein expression get
resolved? What is the optimal expression method? What does the optimal expression
method indicate as the most significant influencing factor? Is this related to the
length of DNA primers and the type of expressed proteins?
Response: Thank you for these insightful questions. As reported previously, the mutual
interference between DNA replication and protein expression has also been observed
in the PURE system, which can be partially alleviated by optimizing the Mg²⁺
concentration (Seo and Ichihashi, ACS Synth. Biol. 2023, 12, 1813-1822). In our study,
we observed a similar phenomenon in LoopReX. Although this interference was not
completely eliminated, we identified a balanced formulation (F3) that represents an
optimal compromise, achieving the highest protein yield together with a relatively high
level of DNA replication (Fig. 2c,d and Supplementary Fig. 8). Particularly, the Mg²⁺
concentration was increased from 12 mM in the original LoopReX to 13.8 mM in the
F3 formulation, suggesting that a slightly higher Mg²⁺ level helps maintain a balanced
and efficient system. This observation aligns with the previous report that “maintaining
an optimal magnesium concentration results in enhanced transcription and translation
while maintaining a certain level of DNA replication in the transcription/translation-
coupled DNA replication reaction” (Seo and Ichihashi, ACS Synth. Biol. 2023, 12,
1813-1822).
We also appreciate your questions regarding the potential effects of primer length and
the type of expressed proteins on LoopReX performance. To address these points, we
conducted additional experiments during the revision.
First, we examined the influence of primer length on DNA replication by synthesizing
random primers ranging from 8 to 16 nucleotides in length. To avoid interference from
endogenous short nucleic acid fragments or T7RNAP-generated abortive transcripts
(typically 3-8 nt), we tested primer-dependent DNA replication in a defined reaction
containing phi29 DNAP, the ssM13 template, and synthetic primers. The results
showed that shorter primers favored DNA replication, with the highest efficiency
achieved using 8-nt primers, which are similar in length to abortive transcripts (see
Figure R1 below).
Second, we evaluated whether the optimized LoopReX system (LoopReX-Opt) could
improve the expression of different protein types beyond the fluorescent reporter
sfGFP. We selected two representative proteins, which were also used in our study (a
scaffold protein, CipB, and a functional enzyme, phi29DNAP), and compared their
expression in the optimized (LoopReX-Opt) and original (LoopReX-Ori) systems. The
results demonstrated that LoopReX-Opt also enhanced the yields of both CipB and
phi29DNAP relative to the original formulation (see Figure R2 below). These findings
indicate that the optimized LoopReX system supports robust protein synthesis across
different protein types.
We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful suggestions, which prompted us to further

To make this point clear, we have revised the relevant sentences in the manuscript as
follows (Page 10):
“The collected data were randomly split, with 80% used for model training and 20%
reserved for independent testing. Then, five-fold cross-validation was performed only
on the training set to assess and enhance the robustness of our models.”
3. How is cross-validation specifically applied in the machine learning part? Is it five-
fold cross-validation on the entire dataset, and then the average performance of
cross-validation is taken as the final result? Or is it first divided into 80/20, and then
five-fold cross-validation is performed on the training set?
Response: Thank you for raising this point of clarification. In our analysis, we adopted
the latter approach. Specifically, the entire dataset was first randomly divided into a
training set (80%) and an independent test set (20%). Five-fold cross-validation was
then performed exclusively on the training set. The training set was further divided into
five approximately equal-sized subsets. In each iteration, one subset was used for
validation, while the other four subsets were used for model training. This procedure
was repeated five times so that each subset served once as the validation set, yielding
five sets of performance metrics. The average performance across these folds was
used for model selection and hyperparameter tuning. After the optimal configuration
was determined, the final model was evaluated on the independent test set, and these
results were reported as the final performance metrics.
To make this point clear, we have revised the relevant sentences in the manuscript as
follows (Page 10):
“The collected data were randomly split, with 80% used for model training and 20%
reserved for independent testing. Then, five-fold cross-validation was performed only
on the training set to assess and enhance the robustness of our models.”
4. If the test set contains conditions that are highly similar to those in the training set
(for example, different concentrations of the same reactant), the model performance
may be overestimated. Although the R² value is high, the ratio of the number of
features to the sample size may be too high, which can easily lead to overfitting. Are
there better methods for dividing the training set and test set?
Response: Thank you for raising this important comment. We agree with your concern
and appreciate the opportunity to further clarify the strategies we employed to minimize
the risk of model overfitting.
First, to minimize bias, we performed a random split of the entire dataset, allocating
80% for model training and 20% for independent testing. All test set data points
remained entirely unseen during training, so model evaluation was conducted
exclusively on previously unobserved conditions.
Second, we employed five-fold cross-validation only within the training set to further
enhance model robustness and reduce the risk of overfitting. In each iteration, one-
fifth of the training data was used for validation, and the model parameters were
optimized based on the averaged performance across all folds.
Third, the XGBoost algorithm inherently includes several regularization mechanisms,
including L1/L2 penalties, tree pruning, and shrinkage, which help to constrain model
complexity and effectively prevent overfitting during the boosting process. Specifically,
new regression trees are added sequentially to minimize residuals while existing trees
remain fixed, ensuring that each iteration contributes only incremental improvements.
Together, these approaches (i.e., randomized data splitting, rigorous cross-validation,
and algorithmic regularization) enabled us to minimize the risk of overfitting and ensure
robust model generalization. Consistent with this, comparative performance metrics
(training R² = 0.99 vs. test R² = 0.81 and 0.88) suggest that our models do not exhibit
significant overfitting in practice.
We are grateful for your insightful feedback and hope this clarification addresses your
concerns.
